knownFor: The Egyptian monk whom Gennadius of Marseilles calls "founder of the Egyptian monasteries", who bound monks to a common rule in shared houses.
datesNote: Born about 292, died 348 (George Schodde; Ernest Cushing Richardson's note to Gennadius) or 346 (Archibald Robertson)
placeNote: Tabennisi, in the Thebaid of Upper Egypt
role: Monk and founder of communal monasticism

keyWorks.title: The Rule of Pachomius
keyWorks.about: the common life of the houses, reported by Palladius and Sozomen and surviving in several later collections, among them an Ethiopic version

traces: Communal monasteries bound by a shared rule, which Palladius counts at seven thousand monks under the rule in his own day.
A rule for women's houses, which Palladius and the Ethiopic version both record living across the river from the men.
remembered: George Schodde, translating the Ethiopic rules in 1885, opens by calling Pachomius "the father of monastic institutions."
Gennadius of Marseilles, continuing Jerome's On Illustrious Men, calls him "a man endowed with apostolic grace both in teaching and in performing miracles."

uncertain: No writing held here is certainly his own. George Schodde thinks the first part of the Ethiopic rules comes close to him: "if not verbatim from his pen, are yet authentic enough for all practical purposes." His life and rule otherwise reach us through his Coptic and Greek Lives, through Palladius of Helenopolis, who tells them as a holy man's story, and through Sozomen, who follows Palladius.

Palladius and Sozomen say an angel gave Pachomius the rule on a tablet, and Gennadius says the rule was "received by angelic dictation." Lowther Clarke, who translated Palladius, reports that the scholar Ladeuze held the Greek Lives of Pachomius more reliable than the rule, thought the angel legendary, and took the lettered groups for Palladius's own invention. Butler, another scholar Clarke cites, did not accept Ladeuze's low view of Palladius's rule and called it "probably the most authentic epitome."
Palladius places Pachomius's own house at Tabennisi. Clarke notes that the head house was by then Pabau, not Tabennisi.

The rule survives in several collections that differ from one another. Schodde says the first part of the Ethiopic version is the same as the Greek form, and judged it reaches back "almost to the days of Pachomius himself," while its later parts are of different origin.

briefReferences: Greek Life, in Daniel Cardon's Latin (Acta Sanctorum, May, vol. 3): headed as by a nearly contemporary monk (80681), and by Archibald Robertson's note written late in the fourth century by one who had known Pachomius (npnf204 30455-30456); Antony, mourning with Pachomius's monks after his death, is praised as the light of the world whose fame reached the emperors, and answers that no community existed when he began (86876-86893).

Before him: Greek Life, he goes to the hermit Palamon to live the solitary life with him (81103-81107); Bohairic Life, tr. Émile Amélineau, he resolves to take up the hermit's life (5330-5331) and Palamon's rule handed down from those before (5424-5427); George Schodde, each monk served God by his own way (pachomius_rules-ethiopic_schodde1885.txt 138).

The shared life: Bohairic Life, the first brothers given rules, the same clothes and food for all (6299-6300, 6333-6336); a steward over each house (6436-6442); the wall, the small church and the houses of the second monastery, with heads and seconds (8175-8178). Jerome's preface to the Rule (PL 23): heads of houses (4388-4397), all eat together (4453), brothers of one trade in one house (4458-4459). Greek Life: nine monasteries in all (86424-86425).

Bohairic Life: his parents pagan (4954-4957); after the persecution, Constantine's call for recruits, and he is taken at twenty (5093-5101); the recruits locked up and fed by men of the town, and the answer to his question (5139-5146); his vow in the night to serve people all the days of his life (5147-5148, 5182-5183); baptized (5240-5241). Greek Life: the persecution over, Constantine, the recruits at about twenty (80977-80992); his vow (81009-81013); born of pagan parents (86417).
Tabennisi, a deserted village by the river, where a voice tells him to build: Bohairic Life 6013-6021; Greek Life 81341-81349.

Bohairic Life: no clergy in his monasteries, for envy and vainglory (6385-6391); the bishop of Denderah asks Athanasius to ordain him, and he hides (6670-6674). Greek Life: he hides among the brothers until Athanasius has passed (82514-82520).

Greek Life: at the church of Latopolis (Esneh), monks and bishops question him over the claim that he reads hidden things (86393-86400); as he finishes, a man driven by an evil spirit bursts in armed with a sword to kill him, and the Lord saves him with the help of those present (86463-86466).

Greek Life: after Easter a plague in all the monasteries (86510-86512, 86572-86574); ill for forty days, he asks for a lighter blanket, is brought one of the best and lightest, and sends it back (86619-86633). The years: 348 by the Bollandists (86728, 86730), 346 by Archibald Robertson (npnf204 5643-5644).
Gennadius, On Illustrious Men 8: Theodore's letters urge back into unity those who broke it after the abbot's death (npnf203 42276-42286).
Palladius, Lausiac History 32, tr. W. K. Lowther Clarke: about seven thousand men under the rule (405), with Clarke's date for the work, 419-420 (657).

Jerome's preface to the Rule of Pachomius (PL 23): the books sent from Alexandria by the priest Silvanus, the Latins in the Thebaid houses and at Metanoia who knew neither Egyptian nor Greek, Leontinus and the brothers pressing him, and the Latin dictated from the Greek version (4335-4354); made also for Eustochium's sisters and his own brothers (4384-4388); dated by its editor to the end of 404 or to 405, after Paula's death (4300-4306).

Ardo, Life of Benedict of Aniane (PL 103): the Concordia regularum, with Benedict's Rule first and the agreeing rules after, to show that his rule rested on the others (30903-30911); the Concordia's sections from the Rule of Pachomius, e.g. 66976; Benedict died in 821 (28836).

quotationOriginals.modern: When I first began to live as a monk, there was no community anywhere in which anyone cared or feared for the salvation of others. Once the persecution was over, each of the early monks trained himself in the monk's life on his own. Later, with God's help, your father did this great good.
quotationOriginals.printed: Etenim quo ego primum tempore Monachum copi agere, nullum uspiam extabat ecenobium, in quo de aliorum salute cura aut metus cuiquam erat ; sed quisque antiquorum Monachorum, persecutione jam finita, privatim in vita sese monastica exercebat, Postea vero Pater vester tantum bonum, Deo adjuvante, effecit.
quotationOriginals.work: Greek Life of Pachomius, in Daniel Cardon's Latin, Acta Sanctorum, May, vol. 3
quotationOriginals.uncertain: Antony's words as the Greek Life reports them, spoken to Pachomius's monks after his death; "your father" is Pachomius. The file is OCR, kept as it stands: "copi" is coepi, "ecenobium" is coenobium; words broken across lines (salu-te, anti-quorum, pri-vatim) are joined. "Etenim" (For) is left out of the rendering. Rendered from Cardon's Latin; the Greek is not held legibly.

quotationOriginals.modern: They are Christian people. They treat us this way out of love for the God of heaven.
quotationOriginals.printed: Ce sont des gens chrétiens : ils agissent ainsi avec nous, par amour pour le Dieu du ciel.
quotationOriginals.work: Bohairic Life of Pachomius, tr. Émile Amélineau, Histoire de saint Pakhôme (Annales du Musée Guimet 17)
quotationOriginals.uncertain: Rendered from Amélineau's French; the Coptic is in the file but its OCR cannot be read. The Greek Life has no speech here (80985-80992).

quotationOriginals.modern: Take this blanket away from here at once. It is not right that I should be better off in anything than the other brothers.
quotationOriginals.printed: Istud, inquit, straguli absque mora hine aufer; non enim iequum est ut in re quapiam melius mihi sit quam Fratribus ceteris.
quotationOriginals.work: Greek Life of Pachomius, in Daniel Cardon's Latin, Acta Sanctorum, May, vol. 3
quotationOriginals.uncertain: The file is OCR, kept as it stands: "hine" is hinc, "iequum" is aequum. "inquit" (he said) is the narrator's, not his words. Rendered from Cardon's Latin; the Greek is not held legibly.
